paper_identity.title: Common dimensional reward deficits across mood and psychotic disorders: a connectome-wide association study
paper_identity.study_type: cross-sectional resting-state fMRI connectome-wide association study

final_report_expectations.research_question: Whether dimensional reward responsivity is associated with functional-connectivity patterns across mood, psychotic, psychosis-risk, and healthy-control groups.
final_report_expectations.study_design: Connectome-wide association study using resting-state functional connectivity and multivariate distance-based matrix regression.
final_report_expectations.population_or_materials: 225 adults after quality assurance from major depressive disorder, bipolar disorder, schizophrenia, psychosis-risk, and healthy-control groups.
methods: Report the Behavioral Activation Scale reward sensitivity subscale as the dimensional reward measure.
Report MDMR/connectome-wide analysis rather than a seed-only case-control analysis.
Preserve the five diagnostic/group counts when sample details are discussed.
primary_findings: Reward deficits were associated with dysconnectivity involving nucleus accumbens, default mode network, and cingulo-opercular network.
Lower reward responsivity was associated with decreased nucleus accumbens-default mode connectivity and increased nucleus accumbens-cingulo-opercular connectivity.
Impaired reward responsivity was associated with default mode hyperconnectivity and diminished default mode-cingulo-opercular connectivity.
secondary_findings: Clinical diagnosis alone did not identify reward-system hubs in MDMR analyses.
Associations were present within each diagnostic category and were directionally consistent but attenuated in healthy controls.
No categorical diagnostic differences in network-level summary measures were observed.
Other BAS subscales showed weaker associations and network effects were not related to disorder-specific illness severity measures.
sensitivity_analysis: Within-group dimensional effects were examined across diagnostic categories.
Analyses excluding healthy controls strengthened the reward-sensitivity associations.
Smoking status and composite medication load were added as covariates and did not alter the findings.
Other BAS subscales and disorder-specific severity measures were evaluated for specificity.
statistical_tests_used: Factor analysis was used to confirm the BAS reward sensitivity subfactor structure in the clinical sample.
Multivariate distance-based matrix regression tested BAS reward sensitivity associations with whole-brain connectivity patterns.
MDMR generated pseudo-F statistics and permutation-based p values at each gray matter voxel.
Cluster correction used voxel height z > 1.64 and cluster extent p < 0.01.
Follow-up seed-based connectivity and network-summary analyses used Pearson correlations and linear regression with clinical group, age, sex, and in-scanner motion covariates.
interpretation: The report should frame findings as transdiagnostic network associations with anhedonia/reward responsivity.
The conclusion should emphasize corticostriatal and large-scale network dysfunction without claiming causal proof.
limitations: Cross-sectional functional connectivity does not establish causality.
Diagnostic groups differed in clinical and medication context, so confounding and generalizability should be handled cautiously.
tables_figures_supplements: Table 1 contains demographic and group information important for interpreting sample composition.
Figures identify connectivity clusters and follow-up network patterns.
final_report_expectations.supplement_availability: The paper cites online data supplement methods/tables; if supplements are not extracted in a run, the synthesis should disclose that supplement-level details were not reviewed.
uniqueness: The paper uses a whole-brain, data-driven CWAS/MDMR approach rather than relying on predefined seed regions.
It evaluates anhedonia dimensionally across mood, psychotic, psychosis-risk, and healthy-control groups in an RDoC-aligned framework.
It links reward deficits to both nucleus accumbens connectivity and large-scale default mode/cingulo-opercular network integration.

critical_claims.claim: The final analytic sample included 225 adults across five groups.
Reward responsivity was measured dimensionally with the Behavioral Activation Scale reward sensitivity subscale.
Reward deficits were linked to nucleus accumbens, default mode network, and cingulo-opercular network dysconnectivity.

report_should_not_claim: Do not claim the study tested a treatment or longitudinal outcome.
Do not claim connectivity differences prove a causal mechanism.
scoring_focus: Preserve sample structure, BAS reward sensitivity, MDMR/connectome-wide method, and network directionality.
Require supplement availability disclosure when online supplement details are not reviewed.
